title: zsh Fundamentals
sub: How the shell reads a line, finds a program, expands what you type, remembers it and starts up
goals: Take a command line apart into command, options and arguments, and say which part the shell handles
Find out what a name resolves to (alias, function, builtin or file) and why one thing shadows another
Predict the result of quoting, globbing, brace, tilde and parameter expansion before pressing Return
Use glob qualifiers and extended globs to select files by type, age and size
Edit and recall command lines with emacs keys, history expansion and search
Build a ~/.zshrc with options, history, prompt, completion, aliases and a function

blocks.text: You type text, press Return, and something happens. Between those two moments the shell does a surprising amount of work: it splits your line into words, rewrites parts of it (aliases, variables, wildcards), decides what each command name means, starts a process and wires up its input and output. Almost every confusing shell moment, such as a wildcard that did not match, a space that split a file name, or a command that is not the one you expected, is a misunderstanding of that sequence. In this chapter you will learn the sequence precisely, then tune zsh until it works for you.

Open Terminal. Everything in `term` blocks is safe to run. Commands that touch `~/lab` assume you built the lab with the Lab Kit in [Setting up your lab](#setup). Reading the output on your own machine is worth more than the output printed here.
Terminal, shell and prompt
Three things get confused. They are separate programs with separate jobs:

blocks.code:
you ──keys──▶ ⟪c:Terminal.app⟫ ──▶ ⟪y:pseudo-terminal⟫ ──▶ ⟪g:zsh⟫ ──fork + exec──▶ ⟪m:ls, ping, python3 ...⟫
                 draws the window,    a kernel device,      reads lines, expands them,    ordinary programs
                 sends your keys,     the two ends of a     runs commands, keeps          with stdin, stdout,
                 shows the output     fake serial cable     variables and history         stderr

items.text: The **terminal emulator** (Terminal.app, iTerm2) is a window. It knows about fonts, colors and tabs. It knows nothing about commands.

The **shell** (`zsh`) is a program that reads lines of text and runs them. It is the default login shell on macOS since Catalina (10.15). It is just a program: you can start another one by typing `zsh`, and leave it with `exit`.

The **prompt** is text the shell prints to say "ready". The default on macOS looks like `learner@MacBook-Pro ~ %`. A `%` ends a zsh prompt for a normal user and `#` appears for root. Only the shell decides what it says, and you can change it (below).

blocks.text: When you press Return, zsh does this, in order: read the line, expand history references, split it into words, perform expansions, work out what the first word means, create a child process (`fork`), replace it with the program (`exec`), wait for it to finish, store its **exit status** in `$?` and print the prompt again. The same loop runs for every command you will ever type.

blocks.code:
$ echo $0
zsh
$ echo $SHELL
/bin/zsh
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin

blocks.text: `$0` is the name of the running shell, `$SHELL` is your login shell as recorded in the system, and `$PATH` is the list of directories searched for programs. On a real Mac, `echo $ZSH_VERSION` prints the exact zsh version (5.9 on current macOS releases).
Anatomy of a command line

The shell splits a line into **words** at unquoted spaces. The first word is the **command**, the rest are its **arguments**. Some arguments start with `-`: those are **options** (or flags) that change behaviour. The shell does not interpret options at all. It passes them to the program, which parses them itself, so each program has its own rules (`ping -c 3` versus `tar -xzf`). The shell only does the expansions in the next sections.

blocks.title: A command line, word by word

tokens.exp: command: the program to run
short option: one dash, one letter (long format)
more short options; usually combinable as -lah (all files, human sizes)
end of options: everything after this is an argument, even if it starts with -
argument: a path; the shell expands ~ before ls sees it

blocks.text: Conventions that hold for most (not all) tools:

items.text: **Short options** are `-x` and can be bundled: `-lah` equals `-l -a -h`. An option that takes a value is usually last in a bundle: `tar -czf out.tgz dir` (the `f` takes the file name).
**Long options** are `--word` or `--word=value`. macOS BSD tools mostly have only short options (`ls -G`, no `--color`), while GNU tools on Linux have many long ones.
**`--`** means "no more options". It is how you handle a file named `-rf`: `rm -- -rf`. Use it when file names come from variables or user input.
A few old tools, such as `ps aux` and `tar xzf`, take options without a dash.

blocks.title: The shell does not know what an option is

blocks.text: `ls -l` and `ls l` differ only because `ls` decides `-l` is an option. To the shell they are both words. That is why an unquoted `*` that expands to a file named `-rf` is dangerous: `rm *` can turn a file name into an option. Prefer `rm -- *` or `rm ./*`.
How zsh finds a command
When the first word is `ls`, which `ls` runs? zsh looks in this order and uses the first match:

items.text: **Reserved words** such as `if`, `for`, `while`, `[[`, `function`.
**Aliases**: text substitutions defined with `alias`.
**Functions**: shell code you defined and named.
**Builtins**: commands implemented inside the shell itself, such as `cd`, `echo`, `export`, `type`, `source`.
**Files in `$PATH`**: the shell searches each directory in order, left to right, and runs the first executable with that name.

blocks.code:
ls  ──▶ reserved word?  ──no──▶ alias?  ──no──▶ function?  ──no──▶ builtin?  ──no──▶ search $PATH
                                                                                              │
                          /opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin ─────┘ first hit wins

blocks.text: Because `$PATH` is searched left to right, order matters. On an Apple Silicon Mac with Homebrew, `/opt/homebrew/bin` comes before `/usr/bin`, so `brew install python` shadows Apple's `/usr/bin/python3`. When a command behaves strangely, the first question is always "which one am I actually running?"

Once zsh has found a file it **remembers** the location in an internal hash table so it does not search again. If you install a new program and the shell says "command not found" or still runs the old one, run `hash -r` (or `rehash`) to clear the table. `hash` alone lists the remembered paths.

blocks.code:
$ type ls
ls is /bin/ls
$ type cd
cd is a shell builtin
$ which awk
/usr/bin/awk
$ type grep
grep is /usr/bin/grep

blocks.text: `cd` is a builtin because it must change the directory of the shell process itself; a child program could never do that.

blocks.name: type
blocks.sum: Show what a name resolves to: alias, function, builtin, reserved word or file.

how.text: In zsh, `type` is the builtin `whence -v`. It applies the lookup order from the previous section and reports the first match. `-a` reports **every** match in order, which is how you discover that Homebrew's program shadows the system one. It is read-only and safe to run on anything.

flags.d: Show all matches, not just the first.
Print only the kind of word (alias, builtin, command, function, reserved).

examples.desc: What is `cd`?
Everything named python3 on the PATH
Print only the paths of all matches
Test whether a tool is installed
examples.code: type jq > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo "jq is installed" || echo "jq is missing"

gotchas: `type -a` lists the match the shell uses *first*. Seeing the same program twice usually means it exists in two PATH directories, such as `/bin/ls` and `/usr/bin/ls`.

blocks.name: which
blocks.sum: Show how a command name will be resolved; in zsh it is a builtin that also prints aliases and function bodies.

how.text: In zsh, `which` is a builtin equal to `whence -c`. It prints the path for a file command, the definition for an alias or function, and `name: shell built-in command` for builtins. Do not confuse it with the external `/usr/bin/which` that macOS also ships, which searches only `$PATH` and prints just a path. In an interactive zsh the builtin wins.

flags.d: Print all matches in `$PATH`, not just the first.

examples.desc: Where is awk?
Show the body of a function you defined
Open the script behind a command in your editor, if it is a file

gotchas: `which` in a shell *script* run by `sh` or bash uses the external program with different output. In scripts use `command -v`.

blocks.name: whence
blocks.sum: zsh's lookup builtin: report how names are resolved, in terse or verbose form.

how.text: `whence name` prints the path of a file command, or the name itself for builtins and reserved words. `-v` gives a sentence (this is what `type` does), `-c` prints the definition of aliases and functions (what `which` does), `-a` lists all matches, `-w` prints just the word type, and `-p` considers only files in `$PATH`, skipping aliases, functions and builtins.

flags.d: Verbose, one sentence per name.
Show every match along the path.
Print the word type: `alias`, `builtin`, `command`, `function`, `reserved`.
Look only in `$PATH`.

examples.desc: Classify a list of words
examples.out:
ls: command
cd: builtin
if: reserved
echo: builtin

examples.desc: List which of several tools are missing
examples.code: for t in jq nmap wget tree; do whence -p $t > /dev/null || echo "missing: $t"; done

blocks.name: command
blocks.sum: Run a command bypassing aliases and functions, or ask how a name would resolve.

how.text: `command name args` runs `name` while skipping any alias or function of that name. That is how a function named `ls` can still call the real one without recursing. `command -v name` prints how the name resolves and **succeeds or fails by exit status**, which makes it the portable way to test whether something exists in scripts that must work in bash and zsh. `-p` searches a default `PATH` that is guaranteed to find the system utilities.

flags.d: Print how the name would be used (a path, an alias, a builtin name); exit status 1 if it is not found.
Verbose version of `-v`.
Use a default PATH, to find the standard utilities.

examples.desc: Test for a tool in a script
examples.code: command -v jq > /dev/null || { echo "install jq first" >&2; exit 1; }

examples.desc: Run the real ls even if you aliased it
Print only the paths of several commands that exist
examples.code: for t in git curl dig; do command -v $t; done

blocks.name: builtin
blocks.sum: Force the shell's own builtin version of a command, skipping functions and external files.

how.text: Some names exist both as builtins and as files (`echo`, `printf`, `kill`, `test`). A function or alias of the same name hides the builtin. `builtin name` calls the builtin directly. It is mainly used inside a function that wraps a builtin, for example a `cd` function that logs directories and then calls `builtin cd "$@"`.

examples.desc: Wrap cd without recursing
Force the builtin echo

blocks.text: Getting help without leaving the terminal
You will look things up constantly, and the fastest source is the machine itself. In increasing order of detail:

items.text: `command --help` or `command -h`: a usage summary. Many BSD tools print usage when you give a bad option; try `ls -Z`.
`whatis command`: one line describing what it is.
`man command`: the full manual page. This is the authoritative source for macOS (BSD) tools.
`man zshbuiltins`, `man zshexpn`, `man zshall`: the zsh manual, split into pages. Builtins such as `cd`, `setopt` and `print` have no manual page of their own; they live in `zshbuiltins`.

blocks.text: Inside a man page the pager is `less`: **Space** next page, **b** back, **/word** search forward (`n` next match, `N` previous), **g** top, **G** bottom, **q** quit.

blocks.name: man
blocks.sum: Open the manual page for a command in a pager.
blocks.syntax: man [section] name      man -k keyword      man -f name

how.text: `man name` finds the page in the manual path and shows it through `less`. Pages are grouped by **section**: 1 user commands, 2 system calls, 3 library functions, 5 file formats, 8 system administration. The same name may exist in several sections, as with `man 5 crontab` (the file format) versus `man 1 crontab` (the command), so you choose with the section number. Read the SYNOPSIS first: square brackets mean optional, `|` means choose one, and `...` means repeatable.

flags.d: Search page names and one-line descriptions for WORD (same as `apropos`).
Show the one-line description of NAME (same as `whatis`).
Use CMD instead of `less` as the pager (`man -P cat ls` dumps the whole page).

examples.desc: The manual for ls
A page from a specific section
Save a page as plain text for searching, stripping the bold formatting
Find which man pages mention a word, then count them

gotchas: macOS man pages describe BSD behaviour. A flag you found on a Linux blog may not exist; the page is the truth for your machine.

blocks.name: apropos
blocks.sum: Search the one-line descriptions of all manual pages for a keyword.

how.text: `apropos` (also `man -k`) consults an index of every page's NAME line. It is how you answer "what is the command that does X?" when you do not know the name. Results look like `name(section) - description`. Search with one or two plain words and narrow from there. If it prints nothing for something that should exist, the index may be stale or missing on your system.

examples.desc: Which commands deal with checksums?
List only the command names that match

blocks.name: whatis
blocks.sum: Print the one-line description of a command.

how.text: `whatis` looks up the NAME line of the manual page. Use it for a quick reminder of what an unfamiliar program does without opening the full page.

examples.desc: What are these?
Describe every program in a folder on your PATH

blocks.name: run-help
blocks.sum: Show help for the command under the cursor; zsh's answer to bash's help builtin.
blocks.syntax: run-help name      (or press Esc then h while typing a command)

how.text: Bash has a `help` builtin; **zsh has no `help` command**. In an interactive zsh, `run-help` is by default just an alias for `man`. If you run `unalias run-help` and `autoload -Uz run-help`, it becomes smarter: it opens the page for external commands, and for builtins and reserved words it shows the right section of the zsh manual. Bound to `Esc` then `h`, it works on a half-typed line: type `git commit`, press `Esc` `h`, and the page opens; when you leave it your line is still there.

examples.desc: Make run-help smart, then use it on a builtin
examples.code: unalias run-help 2>/dev/null; autoload -Uz run-help; run-help setopt

gotchas: Typing `help` in zsh gives `zsh: command not found: help`. Use `man zshbuiltins` for builtins.

blocks.text: Printing text: echo, print and printf
Three commands print text, and they differ in exactly the ways that bite scripts.

blocks.name: echo
blocks.sum: Print its arguments separated by spaces, followed by a newline.

how.text: `echo` joins its arguments with single spaces and adds a newline. **zsh's builtin `echo` interprets backslash escapes by default** (`\t` becomes a tab, `\n` a newline), unlike bash. `-n` omits the trailing newline. Because behaviour differs between zsh, bash and `/bin/echo`, avoid `echo` for anything with backslashes or text beginning with `-`; use `print -r --` or `printf` there.

flags.d: Do not print the trailing newline.
Interpret escapes (already the default in zsh builtin).

examples.desc: See the shell variables at work
Escapes are interpreted in zsh
Append a timestamped line to a log

gotchas: `echo -n` and `echo -e` are not portable across shells. `echo "$var"` misbehaves if `$var` starts with `-`.

blocks.name: print
blocks.sum: zsh's richer builtin for printing: raw mode, one item per line, prompt escapes and variable output.

how.text: `print` is the zsh builtin you want in scripts. `-r` prints arguments raw (no escape interpretation), `-l` prints **one argument per line** (a quick way to inspect a list or an array), `-n` suppresses the newline, and `-P` expands **prompt escapes** such as `%~` and `%F{blue}`, which is how you test a prompt. `--` ends options so text beginning with `-` prints safely.

flags.d: Raw: do not interpret backslashes.
Print each argument on its own line.
No trailing newline.
Perform prompt expansion (`%~`, `%n`, colors).

examples.desc: One file per line from a glob
Test a prompt string without changing your prompt
Count the entries in your PATH
Number the PATH entries

gotchas: `print` is zsh-only. A script that must also run in bash or `sh` should use `printf`.

blocks.name: printf
blocks.sum: Print formatted text using a format string, with no surprises.

how.text: `printf` copies the format string to the output, replacing each conversion such as `%s` (string), `%d` (integer), `%5.1f` (float) and `%x` (hex) with the next argument. It never adds a newline unless the format contains `\n`, and it **reuses the format** while arguments remain, so `printf '%s\n' a b c` prints three lines. It behaves the same in every shell, which makes it the right tool for portable scripts. Numeric conversions are covered in [How computers work](#computers).

flags.d: A string argument.
A decimal integer.
A string left-aligned in a 12-character column.
Newline (also \t tab).

examples.desc: Print one item per line
A two-column table
Format the first three hosts as a table

gotchas: Always give a format string: `printf "$var"` treats the contents of `$var` as a format and breaks on `%`. Use `printf '%s\n' "$var"`.

blocks.text: Quoting: controlling what the shell touches
Before running a command the shell rewrites your words using **expansions**. **Quoting** switches expansion off, wholly or partly, so you can pass special characters literally. There are four tools:

head: Form
What is protected
What still happens
Example
rows: `echo a\ b` is one word `a b`

blocks.code:
$ name=world
$ echo hello $name
hello world
$ echo "hello $name"
hello world
$ echo 'hello $name'
hello $name
$ echo hello\ $name
hello world
$ echo "cost: \$5"
cost: $5

blocks.text: **Always quote variable expansions.** Even though zsh does not split unquoted variables into words or treat their contents as patterns (see below), the habit protects you in bash and `sh`, and in zsh an unquoted *empty* variable disappears as an argument altogether. To include a single quote inside single quotes, close, escape and reopen: `'it'\''s'`.

Copying a command from a web page or chat can bring curly quotes (“ ” ‘ ’) with it. The shell does not treat them as quotes, so you get strange errors or a waiting `>` prompt. Retype the quotes, or paste into a plain-text editor first. If the shell is stuck at a `>` or `dquote>` prompt, press [[Ctrl+C]].
The order of expansion
zsh applies expansions in a fixed sequence. Knowing it explains most puzzles:

items.text: **History expansion**: `!!`, `!$` (interactive only, before anything else).
**Alias expansion**: the first word of a command.
**Process substitution**: `<( )`, `>( )`.
**Parameter expansion**: `$var`, `${var:-x}`.
**Command substitution**: `$( )`.
**Arithmetic expansion**: `$(( ))`.
**Brace expansion**: `{a,b}`, `{1..5}`.
**Filename expansion**: `~`, `~user`, `=cmd`.
**Filename generation (globbing)**: `*`, `?`, `[...]`.
**Quote removal**: the quotes themselves are deleted.

blocks.text: Two consequences: because brace expansion comes after parameter expansion, `{$a..$b}` works as a range in zsh (it does not in bash), and because quote removal is last, quotes protect their content through all the earlier stages. One zsh difference from bash: a `*` that arrives from a variable is **not** globbed, even unquoted (`x='*.txt'; echo $x` prints `*.txt`), unless you ask with `${~x}` or `setopt GLOB_SUBST`.
Tilde and brace expansion

`~` becomes your home directory, `~+` the current directory, `~-` the previous directory and `~name` the home of user `name`. Braces generate lists **before** any file lookup, whether or not the files exist, so they are the quick way to create or name many things at once:

blocks.code:
$ echo ~
/Users/learner
$ echo {1..3} file{a,b}.txt
1 2 3 filea.txt fileb.txt
$ echo report-{2025,2026}-{01,02}.csv
report-2025-01.csv report-2025-02.csv report-2026-01.csv report-2026-02.csv

blocks.text: Because parameters expand first, variables work inside a range in zsh: with `a=1 b=3`, `{$a..$b}` gives `1 2 3` (bash leaves it as literal text; there you need `seq`). Zero padding works with a leading zero on either end: `{01..10}`.
Globbing (filename generation)
A **glob** is a pattern the shell expands into the sorted list of matching file names. The program never sees the pattern, only the result. Globs match names, never contents.

head: Pattern
Matches
Example
rows: any string of characters, but not a leading `.` and not `/`
one character from the set, range or not in the set
not a glob but brace expansion, applied first

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ ls data/*.log
data/delta.log  data/gamma.log
$ ls data/[a-b]*
data/alpha.txt  data/beta.txt

data/archive:
old.log
$ ls *.zzz
zsh: no matches found: *.zzz

blocks.text: The last command fails with `zsh: no matches found: *.zzz`. This is a **difference from bash**: in bash an unmatched glob stays as literal text, but zsh treats a pattern that matches nothing as an **error** and does not run the command (the `NOMATCH` option). That protects you from `rm *.tmp` acting on a literal `*.tmp`, but it will surprise you in scripts and when a command expects to receive the pattern, as with `find . -name *.log`. Quote it (`'*.log'`), or tell zsh that no match is fine.
Extended globs and qualifiers
zsh globbing goes far beyond other shells. Turn on `setopt EXTENDED_GLOB` (put it in `~/.zshrc`) for these extra operators:

head: Pattern
Meaning
Example
rows: match, then remove names matching the exclude
zero or more, one or more of `x`

blocks.text: **Glob qualifiers** go in parentheses at the *end* of the pattern and filter by file properties instead of name. They work in plain zsh with no option needed.

head: Qualifier
Selects
Example
rows: sort by modification time, newest first (`Om` oldest first)
size larger than 100 KB (`Lm` megabytes, `L0` empty files)
modified within the last hour (`md-7` days, `mw-1` weeks)
no error if nothing matches (null glob)

blocks.text: Qualifiers combine by writing them in sequence: `*(.om[1,3])` means regular files, newest first, the first three. This replaces many `find` and `ls | sort | head` pipelines, and combined with the recursive pattern from the table above it searches whole trees:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ print -l *(.)
README.txt
access.log
hosts.txt
ips.txt
notes.txt
ping.log
scan.txt
users.csv
$ print -l *(/)
data
$ print -l **/*.log(.)
access.log
data/archive/old.log
data/delta.log
data/gamma.log
ping.log
$ print -l *(.om[1,2])
users.csv
scan.txt

blocks.text: (The last two lines depend on the modification times on your Mac.) A qualifier is zsh-only syntax, so scripts meant for bash cannot use it.

tokens.exp: zsh builtin that prints; -l puts each argument on its own line
one item per line
descend through every subdirectory
name pattern: names ending in .log
start of qualifiers
regular files only
order by modification time, newest first
keep the first three results
end of qualifiers

blocks.text: Use `setopt NULL_GLOB` for a whole script, or add `(N)` to one pattern, when "no files" is a normal situation: `for f in *.tmp(N); do rm -- "$f"; done` does nothing instead of failing when there are no `.tmp` files.
Variables and parameters, briefly

You assign with `name=value`, with **no spaces around `=`**, and read with `$name`. A variable you want child programs to see must be exported (see the `export` card below). Parameter expansion has modifiers for defaults and trimming that you will use constantly; the full set is covered in [Scripting](#scripting).

head: Form
Result
Example with `v=report-2026.csv`
rows: the value, or `default` if unset or empty
remove the shortest match from the end
remove the shortest match from the front

blocks.text: Two big differences from bash

**No word splitting of unquoted variables.** In bash, `x="a b"; for i in $x` runs twice. In zsh it runs **once**: `$x` stays one word. To split deliberately, use `${=x}`. Most bash scripts you find online were written assuming splitting, so copy them with care.

blocks.code:
$ x="a b"
$ for i in $x; do echo "[$i]"; done
[a b]

blocks.text: **Arrays are 1-indexed.** In bash the first element is `arr[0]`; in zsh it is `arr[1]`, and `$arr[0]` is empty. Negative indexes count from the end, and `$arr[2,3]` slices. Unlike bash, `$arr` with no index expands to all elements.

blocks.code:
$ arr=(alpha beta gamma)
$ echo $arr[1] $arr[-1] ${#arr} $arr[2,3]
alpha gamma 3 beta gamma

blocks.text: zsh also has **`$path`**, an array tied to `$PATH`: `path=(~/bin $path)` puts a directory first on the search path. And `$PWD`, `$OLDPWD`, `$?` (last exit status), `$$` (this shell's PID) and `$0` are set by the shell itself.
Aliases and functions

An **alias** replaces the first word of a command with other text. It is for shortcuts. A **function** is shell code with a name and can take arguments. When you need `$1`, a pipe in the middle, or more than one command, write a function.

blocks.name: alias
blocks.sum: Define a shorthand for a command line, or list the aliases that exist.

how.text: `alias ll='ls -lah'` makes `ll` expand to `ls -lah` before the line is parsed. Aliases apply only to the **first word** of a command and exist only in the current shell session, so put the ones you want permanently in `~/.zshrc`. Always use single quotes so nothing expands at definition time. `alias` alone lists everything; `unalias name` removes one. zsh adds **global aliases** (`alias -g L='| less'`, expanded anywhere in the line) and **suffix aliases** (`alias -s txt=nano`, so typing `notes.txt` opens it).

flags.d: Global alias: expands anywhere on the line.
Suffix alias: runs the command on a file with that extension.

examples.desc: A long listing with human sizes
A listener-finder you will use in the network chapters
Show only the aliases that mention ls
Count your aliases

gotchas: An alias cannot take arguments in the middle. `alias count='wc -l $1'` does not work; use a function. To bypass an alias once, write `\ls` or `command ls`.

blocks.text: Functions live in the same place as aliases and are defined with `name() { ... }`. Arguments arrive as `$1`, `$2`, ..., all of them as `"$@"`:

tokens.exp: name followed by () : this defines a function called mkcd
start of the body
create the directory named by the first argument, with parents; -- guards against names starting with -
run the next command only if that one succeeded
change into it
the list of commands must end with ; (or a newline) before the closing brace

blocks.text: `which mkcd` or `type mkcd` shows it afterwards. Reload your configuration with `source ~/.zshrc` after editing it.

blocks.name: autoload
blocks.sum: Mark a function to be loaded from a file on first use, instead of defined up front.

how.text: zsh ships many functions as files in directories listed in the array `$fpath`. `autoload -Uz name` declares the name; the file is read the first time you call it, which keeps start-up fast. `-U` stops alias expansion inside the function and `-z` selects zsh-style loading. You will meet it in `autoload -Uz compinit && compinit` (the completion system) and `autoload -Uz colors && colors`.

flags.d: Suppress alias expansion while loading the function.
Load the function in zsh style.

examples.desc: Turn on the completion system
Make your own functions loadable from a folder
See which directories zsh searches for functions

blocks.text: Line editing and history
zsh reads your line with its own editor, **ZLE**. The default keymap on macOS is emacs-style, and a handful of keys will double your speed:

head: Keys
Action
rows: jump to the start / end of the line
back / forward one character (the arrow keys also work)
back / forward one word (Esc then `b` / `f` in any terminal)
delete the word before the cursor
delete from the cursor to the start of the line
delete from the cursor to the end of the line
paste (yank) the last thing you deleted
search history backwards as you type; press again for the next match
cancel a search or the current line
abort the current line or stop a running command
at an empty prompt: exit the shell

blocks.text: Keys such as `Alt+B` and `Alt+F` need a Meta key. In Terminal.app go to Settings, Profiles, Keyboard and tick **Use Option as Meta key**; otherwise Option+letter types characters like `∫`. In iTerm2 the setting is Profiles, Keys, "Left Option key: Esc+". Esc followed by the letter always works as a fallback: tap Esc, then `b`.
History
zsh records each command you run. Three ways to reuse them, from quickest:

items.text: **Search with [[Ctrl+R]]**: start typing any part of an old command. Press [[Ctrl+R]] again for older matches, Return to run, or an arrow key to edit first.
**History expansion** with `!`: the shell replaces these *before* running the line.

head: Expression
Expands to
Typical use
rows: the last argument of the previous command
the first argument of the previous command
reuse the first of several files
the second argument of the previous command
the most recent command that started with `ls`
the previous command with the first `old` replaced by `new`

items.text: **The `history` and `fc` builtins**, below, to list or edit.

blocks.text: Press [[Tab]] after typing `!!` or `!$` and zsh shows the expansion in your line so you can check it before pressing Return. Make that your habit with `sudo !!`.

blocks.name: history
blocks.sum: List the commands you have run; in zsh it is shorthand for `fc -l`.

how.text: By default `history` shows only the **last 16** commands in zsh, which surprises people coming from bash. `history 0` shows everything in memory, `history -20` the last twenty. With the `EXTENDED_HISTORY` option set, `-i` adds ISO timestamps and `-E` European-style ones. Numbers on the left are event numbers you can use as `!123`.

flags.d: Show all history, from event 1.
Show the last N events (for example `-20`).
Show timestamps (requires EXTENDED_HISTORY).

examples.desc: The last 20 commands
Your ten most used commands
examples.code: history 0 | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

examples.desc: Find an earlier curl command

gotchas: The saved file (`$HISTFILE`) is only written under some options. Without `SHARE_HISTORY` or `INC_APPEND_HISTORY`, commands from one Terminal tab are saved only when that shell exits and can be overwritten by another tab. See the history options below.

blocks.name: fc
blocks.sum: List, edit and re-run history entries.

how.text: `fc -l` lists history (the same as `history`); `-n` hides the numbers so the output can be fed to other commands. `fc` with no options opens the previous command in `$EDITOR`, lets you change it, and runs it when you save and quit, which is the right way to fix a long command. `fc -e - ` (zsh builtin `r`) re-runs the previous command immediately, optionally with a substitution.

flags.d: List instead of editing.
Omit event numbers.
Re-run without editing (substitute with `old=new`).

examples.desc: Edit the last command in your editor
Re-run the last command with a substitution
Copy the last command to the clipboard

blocks.text: History options

zsh's defaults are tiny. Without configuration zsh keeps only **30** commands and writes **none** to disk, though macOS ships an `/etc/zshrc` that sets `HISTFILE` and larger limits, as you can check with `echo $HISTFILE $HISTSIZE $SAVEHIST`. These are the settings most people add to `~/.zshrc`:

head: Setting
Effect
rows: every tab writes immediately and reads other tabs' commands
do not store a command that repeats the previous one
do not store commands that start with a space, a quick way to keep a secret out of history
also store the time and duration of each command

blocks.text: Options: setopt, unsetopt and set

zsh's behaviour is controlled by roughly 190 **options**, each on or off. Names ignore case and underscores, so `AUTO_CD`, `autocd` and `auto_cd` are the same option. Options prefixed with `NO_` mean off: `setopt NO_CLOBBER` equals `unsetopt CLOBBER`.

blocks.name: setopt
blocks.sum: Turn zsh options on (setopt) or off (unsetopt); with no arguments setopt lists the ones that differ from the defaults.

how.text: An option changes a shell behaviour for the current session; put the `setopt` line in `~/.zshrc` to make it permanent. `setopt` alone prints options that are currently *on* and non-default, `set -o` prints every option with its state, and `[[ -o autocd ]]` tests one in a script. A script that depends on options should set them at its top, because the interactive options in your `.zshrc` are not loaded for scripts.

flags.d: Typing a directory name alone changes into it (`~/lab` or `..`).
Offer to fix a mistyped command name ("zsh: correct 'gti' to 'git' [nyae]?").
Enable `^`, `~`, `#` and `(#i)` in patterns.
Skip consecutive duplicate history entries.
Share history live between all open shells.
Allow `#` comments on the command line.
Refuse to overwrite an existing file with `>` (use `>|` to force).

examples.desc: Turn on a few helpful options for this session
Check whether an option is on
List the options that are on, sorted
Show which options a clean shell (no startup files) has changed from the defaults

gotchas: **Pasting comments fails by default.** Interactive zsh does not recognise `#` as a comment, so `ls # list` runs `ls` with the arguments `#` and `list`, and a pasted line starting with `#` gives `zsh: command not found: #`. `setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS` fixes it.
`setopt CORRECT_ALL` also tries to correct file names and can "fix" a valid argument you meant literally. Many people prefer `CORRECT` only (commands), not `CORRECT_ALL`.

blocks.text: Environment variables

Every process has an **environment**: a set of `NAME=value` strings it inherits from its parent. The shell keeps ordinary **shell variables** to itself, and passes only **exported** ones to the programs it starts. That is why `PATH`, `HOME`, `EDITOR` and `LANG` work everywhere: the shell exported them.

blocks.name: export
blocks.sum: Mark a variable so programs started from this shell receive it in their environment.

how.text: `export NAME=value` sets the variable and marks it for export. From then on, every child process inherits a copy; changes the child makes are not seen by the parent. `export` alone lists the exported variables. A one-shot form, `NAME=value command`, sets the variable only for that single command. Exports last for the shell session, so put the ones you want everywhere into `~/.zprofile` (for `PATH`) or `~/.zshrc`.

examples.desc: Add a folder of your own scripts to the front of the path
Set a variable for one command only
Show which exported variables mention your home folder

anat.exp: the variable name, no dollar sign when assigning
assignment; no spaces on either side
new value: the old PATH is appended after your folder, quoted to keep it one word

gotchas: `export PATH=...` replaces the whole path. Always include `$PATH` (or `$path` in zsh array form) unless you mean to remove everything else.

blocks.name: env
blocks.sum: Print the environment, or run a command with a modified one.

how.text: With no arguments `env` prints every exported variable, one `NAME=value` per line. With assignments and a command, it runs the command with those variables set. `-i` starts the command with an **empty** environment, the best way to test whether a script depends on something it did not declare. `printenv NAME` prints just the value of one variable and exits non-zero if it is not set.

flags.d: Start with an empty environment.
Remove NAME from the command's environment.

examples.desc: See the values the shell passes down
Run a command in a clean environment
Get one value for use in another command
Number of exported variables

blocks.text: Startup files

When zsh starts it reads configuration files in a fixed order. Which ones run depends on two properties of the shell: is it a **login** shell and is it **interactive**. Terminal.app starts a **login** shell for every new window and tab, so on macOS both the login and interactive files run each time you open one.

head: File
When it is read
Put here
rows: **every** zsh, including scripts and `ssh host command`
almost nothing; only variables every program must see
options, history, prompt, aliases, functions, completion, key bindings

blocks.code:
login + interactive shell (a new Terminal tab):

   /etc/zshenv ─▶ ~/.zshenv ─▶ /etc/zprofile ─▶ ~/.zprofile ─▶ /etc/zshrc ─▶ ~/.zshrc ─▶ /etc/zlogin ─▶ ~/.zlogin
                                  │
                                  └ on macOS runs path_helper: builds PATH from /etc/paths and /etc/paths.d/*

blocks.text: On macOS, `/etc/zprofile` runs `/usr/libexec/path_helper`, which rebuilds `PATH` from `/etc/paths` and `/etc/paths.d` and runs *after* `~/.zshenv`. A `PATH` you set in `.zshenv` can therefore be reordered. Setting it in `~/.zprofile` (read after `/etc/zprofile`) is reliable. Scripts that you run with `./script.zsh` skip `.zshrc` entirely, which is why aliases from `.zshrc` do not exist inside scripts.

blocks.name: source
blocks.sum: Run the commands in a file inside the current shell, so its variables, aliases and functions stay.

how.text: Running `./script.zsh` starts a **child** process, which cannot change your shell. `source file` (or its short form `. file`) reads the file and executes each line *in your shell*, so assignments, `cd`, aliases, functions and options take effect. It is how you reload `~/.zshrc` after editing it, and how a project can provide a set of environment variables.

examples.desc: Reload your configuration
Load variables from a file for this session
Load only the alias lines from a file

gotchas: A syntax error in `.zshrc` stops the rest of the file from loading. Test with `zsh -n ~/.zshrc` (syntax check only, nothing is run) before opening a new tab.

blocks.name: zsh
blocks.sum: Start a new zsh shell, run a command or script with it, or check its syntax.

how.text: `zsh` with no arguments starts a nested interactive shell; `exit` returns to the previous one. `zsh -c 'command'` runs one command string and exits, which is how you try snippets in isolation. `zsh script.zsh` runs a file without needing the execute bit. `-f` starts with **no startup files**, a clean shell to test whether a problem comes from your own configuration. `-n` only checks syntax. `-x` prints each command as it runs, with expansions applied.

flags.d: Run CMD and exit.
Read the commands but do not execute them (syntax check).
Trace: print each command before it runs.
Do not read startup files (clean shell for debugging).
Force interactive mode.
Act as a login shell.

examples.desc: Test a command in a clean shell
Syntax-check your configuration
Time how long your shell takes to start
See every command a script runs

gotchas: `zsh -f` is the first thing to try when "it works on my machine" fails: if the problem disappears, a line in your own `~/.zshrc` or `~/.zshenv` is the cause.

blocks.name: exit
blocks.sum: Leave the current shell (or script) with an exit status.

how.text: In an interactive shell `exit` (or [[Ctrl+D]] on an empty line) ends the session and closes the tab if it was the last one. In a script `exit N` stops the script and reports status `N` (0 means success) to whoever ran it. If you have stopped or background jobs, zsh warns once ("you have suspended jobs") and exits if you repeat it. Inside a nested shell started with `zsh`, `exit` only returns to the parent.

examples.desc: Leave with a failure status in a script
See the status of the last command

blocks.name: clear
blocks.sum: Clear the terminal screen.

how.text: `clear` asks the terminal to erase the visible text and move the prompt to the top. In Terminal.app, [[Cmd+K]] also clears the scrollback, and [[Ctrl+L]] clears the screen but keeps the line you are typing and the scrollback, which makes it the one to use while editing a command. Clearing hides output; it does not delete history or files.

examples.desc: Clear the screen

blocks.text: Tab completion

Press [[Tab]] and zsh completes a command name, a file name, a variable or, with the completion system on, an **option** or the **argument type** a command expects (a git branch, a running process id, an SSH host from `~/.ssh/config`). Completions come from functions in `$fpath`, loaded by `compinit`. The macOS default configuration does **not** call `compinit`, so out of the box you get only basic file completion. Turn the full system on in `~/.zshrc`:

blocks.code:
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select
zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-z}={A-Za-z}'

blocks.text: `zstyle` configures completion by *context*. The first line after `compinit` makes repeated [[Tab]] presses open a selectable menu; the second makes lower-case input match upper-case names. After `brew install` of a tool, completion scripts are installed to `$(brew --prefix)/share/zsh/site-functions`; add it to `fpath` before `compinit`: `fpath=($(brew --prefix)/share/zsh/site-functions $fpath)`.
Prompt customization
The prompt is the value of the `PROMPT` variable (also called `PS1`), containing text and **prompt escapes** that start with `%`. `RPROMPT` is an optional prompt on the right edge.

head: Escape
Meaning
rows: host name up to the first dot
current directory, with your home as `~`
only the last component of the directory
`%` for a normal user, `#` for root
exit status of the previous command
start and stop a foreground color (names or numbers 0-255)
if the last status was 0 show A, else B

blocks.title: A prompt with a status-colored symbol

tokens.exp: assign the prompt variable (single quotes so zsh evaluates it later)
green user@host, then reset color
blue current directory
choose green if the last command succeeded, red if it failed
the % or # symbol, then reset the color
a trailing space so your typing does not touch the symbol

blocks.text: Test a prompt string with `print -P` before you commit to it, and put the final `PROMPT=` line in `~/.zshrc`:

blocks.code: print -P '%F{green}%n@%m%f %F{blue}%~%f %(?.%F{green}.%F{red})%#%f '

blocks.text: To show the git branch you need `vcs_info`, a function you load with `autoload -Uz vcs_info` and enable with `precmd() { vcs_info }` plus `setopt PROMPT_SUBST`; see `man zshcontrib` when you want it.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Spaces around `=`.** `x = 5` runs a command named `x`. Write `x=5`.
**Unquoted file names with spaces.** `touch my notes.txt` makes two files. Quote it: `touch "my notes.txt"`.
**Expecting bash behaviour for `$x` splitting and `arr[0]`.** zsh does not split and counts from 1.
**A pattern that matches nothing.** `zsh: no matches found` is the shell protecting you. Quote it for `find`, or use `(N)`.
**Pasting a command with a comment.** Needs `setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS`.
**Editing `.zshrc` and wondering why nothing changed.** The file is read when the shell starts. Run `source ~/.zshrc` or open a new tab.
**Putting an alias in a script.** Aliases are for your interactive session, not for scripts; use a function or the full command.
**`PATH` clobbered.** `export PATH=/new/dir` without `:$PATH` makes `ls` vanish. Open a new tab to recover, then fix the line.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Which one runs?

task.text: For each of the names `echo`, `cd`, `ls`, `python3` and `if`, find out what the shell resolves it to (alias, function, builtin, reserved word or file and its path). For `ls` and `python3`, also print **all** places the name exists, in search order.

hints: `type` reports one name at a time; `whence -w` prints just the kind.
blocks.solution:
whence -w echo cd ls python3 if
type -a ls
type -a python3

why.text: The first command shows kinds (`builtin`, `command`, `reserved`). `type -a` follows the search order, so the first line is what actually runs. Two lines for `python3` mean Homebrew or another install shadows Apple's.

blocks.title: Predict, then check

task.text: In zsh, what does each line print? Work them out before running anything.

hints: zsh does not split unquoted variables. Braces expand before anything else.
blocks.solution:
[a b]
a1 a2 b1 b2
$HOME 5
x z 3
/Users/yourname/lab

why.text: The loop runs once because `$f` is not split. Braces multiply left to right. Single quotes block `$HOME` while double quotes still allow arithmetic. Arrays start at 1, `[-1]` is the last element, `${#arr}` is the count, and `~` expands to your home directory.

blocks.title: Glob qualifiers on the lab

task.text: Using only `print -l` and glob qualifiers, from `~/lab`: (a) list the regular files in `data`, (b) list the sub-directories of `data`, (c) list `.log` files at any depth under `~/lab`, (d) show the single most recently modified regular file in `~/lab`, (e) list files in `~/lab` larger than 1 KB.

hints: `(.)` regular files, `(/)` directories, `**/` for any depth, `(om[1])` the newest.
For the size, `(Lk+1)` means larger than 1 kilobyte.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab
print -l data/*(.)
print -l data/*(/)
print -l **/*.log(.)
print -l *(.om[1])
print -l *(.Lk+1)

why.text: Qualifiers filter by file attributes, replacing `find` or `ls | sort | head` pipelines. They combine in sequence: `(.om[1])` is "regular files, newest first, first one".

blocks.title: Break the quoting, then fix it

task.text: In a scratch folder, `mkdir -p ~/lab/scratch && cd ~/lab/scratch`. Run these four commands, observe what goes wrong in each, and fix each one.

task.code:
touch my notes.txt
echo Total: $5 files
ls *.zzz
echo "It's $(date +%Y)" 'cost $5'

task.text: After the first command look at `ls`: you should have two files, not one. Remove them, then repeat with the fix.

hints: Spaces split words; `$5` is a positional parameter that is empty; an unmatched glob is an error in zsh.
blocks.solution:
rm -- my notes.txt
touch "my notes.txt"
echo 'Total: $5 files'
ls *.zzz(N)
echo "It's $(date +%Y)" 'cost $5'
ls

why.text: Quotes keep `my notes.txt` as one word. Single quotes stop `$5` expanding. `(N)` turns "no match" into an empty result. The last line already worked: double quotes allow `$(...)`, an apostrophe is harmless inside them, and single quotes keep `$5` literal.

blocks.title: History without retyping

task.text: Without retyping paths: run `mkdir -p ~/lab/hist/a/b/c`, then change into the new directory using history expansion, then run `ls /nonexistent` (it fails) and re-run your previous directory command with `!`-expansion by name. Finally, use [[Ctrl+R]] to find the `mkdir` command again and add a `-v` before running it.

hints: `cd !$` uses the last argument of the previous command.
`!mkdir` re-runs the most recent command that began with `mkdir`.
blocks.solution:
mkdir -p ~/lab/hist/a/b/c
cd !$
pwd
ls /nonexistent
!mkdir
(Ctrl+R, type mkdir, press Return or an arrow key to edit)

why.text: History expansion is replaced before the command runs, so `cd !$` becomes `cd ~/lab/hist/a/b/c`. Press Tab after `!$` to see the expansion first, a habit that makes `sudo !!` safe.

questions.q: In what order does zsh look for the meaning of a command name?

options.text: Reserved words, aliases, functions, builtins, then files in PATH
Builtins, aliases, reserved words, PATH files

questions.why: Reserved words and aliases are checked first, then functions and builtins, and only then the directories in `$PATH`. That is why an alias or function can hide a program of the same name.

questions.q: What happens when you run `echo *.zzz` in zsh and nothing matches?

options.text: zsh prints `no matches found` and does not run the command

questions.why: The `NOMATCH` option makes an unmatched pattern an error. Use quotes, `(N)` or `setopt NULL_GLOB` to change that.

questions.q: `x="a b"; for i in $x; do echo $i; done` runs the loop how many times in zsh?
questions.why: zsh does not split unquoted variables into words. Use `${=x}` to split on whitespace.

questions.q: Which glob lists only regular files, newest first, and keeps the first three?
questions.why: `.` selects regular files, `om` orders by modification time newest first, and `[1,3]` slices the first three results. `Om` would be oldest first.

questions.q: Which file should hold your Homebrew `eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"` line on macOS, and why?
questions.why: `.zprofile` is read by login shells (every Terminal tab) after `/etc/zprofile` has run `path_helper`, so your `PATH` changes are not reordered afterwards.

questions.q: Which line pastes safely from a web page that contains `# comment` lines?
questions.why: Interactive zsh does not treat `#` as a comment by default, which gives `command not found: #` when you paste annotated commands.

blocks.text: You will build a configuration in a scratch file first, test it in a subshell, and only then install it as your real `~/.zshrc`. That way a typo never leaves you with a broken shell.
Step 1: Back up and start a draft

blocks.code:
[[ -f ~/.zshrc ]] && cp ~/.zshrc ~/.zshrc.bak
mkdir -p ~/lab/zsh && cd ~/lab/zsh

blocks.text: Create `zshrc-draft` in PyCharm or with `nano zshrc-draft`, and add the sections below one at a time.
Step 2: Options and history

blocks.code:
# ---- options ----
setopt AUTO_CD INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS EXTENDED_GLOB NO_CLOBBER

# ---- history ----
HISTFILE=~/.zsh_history
HISTSIZE=50000
SAVEHIST=50000
setopt SHARE_HISTORY HIST_IGNORE_DUPS HIST_IGNORE_SPACE EXTENDED_HISTORY

blocks.text: Step 3: Completion, aliases and a function
Append to the same file:

blocks.code:
# ---- completion ----
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select
zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-z}={A-Za-z}'

# ---- aliases ----
export CLICOLOR=1
alias ll='ls -lah'
alias ports='lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN'
alias reload='source ~/.zshrc'

# ---- functions ----
mkcd() { mkdir -p -- "$1" && cd -- "$1"; }

blocks.text: `CLICOLOR=1` turns on colors in macOS `ls` (it is how BSD `ls` learns to colorize, since `--color` does not exist).
Step 4: The prompt

blocks.code:
# ---- prompt ----
PROMPT='%F{green}%n@%m%f %F{blue}%~%f %(?.%F{green}.%F{red})%#%f '
RPROMPT='%F{8}%*%f'

blocks.text: Step 5: Test before you install

blocks.code:
zsh -n zshrc-draft && echo "syntax ok"
zsh -i -c 'source ~/lab/zsh/zshrc-draft; alias ll; type mkcd; print -P "$PROMPT"'

blocks.text: `zsh -n` checks syntax without running anything. The second command loads the draft in a throw-away interactive shell and shows the alias, the function and the expanded prompt. When both look right:

blocks.code:
cp ~/lab/zsh/zshrc-draft ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

blocks.text: Open a new Terminal tab and confirm the prompt changed and `ll` works. If something is wrong, restore with `cp ~/.zshrc.bak ~/.zshrc`.

Add `export EDITOR=nano`. Add an alias `lab='cd ~/lab'` (or rely on `AUTO_CD` and type `~/lab`). Show only the last directory name with `%1~`. Add a function `up() { cd "${1:-..}"; }`. Time your shell startup with `time zsh -i -c exit` before and after.
Try it in the practice terminal

This terminal is a simulation with the same lab files as your `~/lab`. It understands the quoting, globbing and brace expansion from this chapter. Features that need a real zsh, such as glob qualifiers, `setopt` and history expansion, are for your own Terminal.
Next: [Files, folders and permissions](#files) shows you where everything lives on a Mac and how to create, find, move, compress and protect it.

terms.def: A program that reads commands, expands them and starts other programs (zsh on macOS)
The window application (Terminal.app, iTerm2) that displays the shell's text and sends your keystrokes
The text the shell prints to show it is ready for a command
A command implemented inside the shell itself, such as cd or echo, instead of a separate file
A text shortcut that replaces the first word of a command line
A pattern with wildcards that the shell expands to matching file names
A zsh suffix in parentheses that filters glob results by file type, age or size
The shell rewriting part of a command line (variables, braces, tilde, globs) before running it
A shell started as part of logging in; Terminal.app starts one for each tab
The array of directories zsh searches for autoloaded functions and completions
The Zsh Line Editor that handles your typing, history search and key bindings
The use of ! forms such as !! and !$ to reuse parts of earlier commands
A named on/off switch for shell behaviour, set with setopt and unsetopt
An exported NAME=value pair that child processes inherit
